title: The chef who cooks in your kitchen

beats.say: Why do strong engineers lose job offers they should have won?

Because half of a typical interview loop is not technical. There is a hiring manager chat, a behavioral round, and often a product case. Think of a driving test. Knowing the engine does not help if you cannot read the road.

chip.text: Half the loop is not technical

beats.say: Now picture a personal chef who moves into your kitchen. They ask what your family likes, then cook it right there. A forward deployed engineer does that with software, inside a customer's company.

chip.text: Listen first, then build on site

beats.say: That job barely existed a year ago. Now it is everywhere. Listening, explaining and building are the skills it rewards.

check.q: What does a forward deployed engineer do?
opts: Works inside a customer's environment, learns their need and ships software for them
Only answers support tickets from head office
Designs chips for cloud servers
check.why: The role is defined by being embedded with the customer, finding what they actually need, and shipping production software there.

work: Write down two stories where you listened to a business team and changed what you built.
Practise explaining your last project to a non-technical friend in 60 seconds.

title: A week in the life, and what interviews copy

beats.say: How does a forward deployed engineer spend a week?

First, sit with the customer and find the real problem, not the one written in the ticket. Second, build a working solution on their data. Third, ship it to production and stay until people actually use it.

Postings for this role rose from 643 to 5,330 in twelve months. That is about eight times. The top skills are Python, AI agents, TypeScript, AWS and LLMs. SQL and a modern data stack are simply assumed.
Interviewers test the same loop. Atlassian asks why click-through rose while conversions fell. You must ask questions first, then reason to a cause, then recommend.

check.q: Why does a case question like rising click-through with falling conversions reward asking questions first?
opts: Interviewers dislike quick answers
The real cause depends on definitions and data you do not yet know
Questions buy time to recall the formula
check.why: Like the customer's ticket, the stated problem hides the real one. Clarifying definitions and data narrows the cause before you recommend.

work: Practise one metric puzzle aloud: ask three clarifying questions before any theory.
Check that your SQL and Python are sharp, since postings assume them.

title: Case traps and reading the market

beats.say: Click-through went up but conversions fell. What do you say first?

Not a guess. Check the data first. Did the metric definition change? Did the traffic mix shift, with cheap clicks from people who never meant to buy? Is checkout broken? Name causes, then say how you would test each.

chip.text: Name causes, then a test for each

beats.say: Candidates fail by diving into one theory, or by speaking jargon to a non-technical buyer, like when Google asks you to sell its cloud to a business leader.
Also read the job market carefully. Postings are not hires. And location matters: in India, Google Cloud, Sarvam AI and Accenture were hiring, but Palantir, OpenAI and Anthropic had none then.

check.q: A product lead says conversions fell while click-through rose. Best first response?
opts: Say the landing page is bad and propose a redesign
Clarify metric definitions and traffic mix, list causes, and say how to test each
Ask for a bigger ad budget
check.why: A structured list of testable causes beats an early guess. It shows you will not act on an unverified theory.

work: Build a checklist for metric puzzles: definition, population, funnel step, timing.
Rewrite one technical explanation with no jargon for a buyer.

title: Is this role your best bet?

beats.say: Is a forward deployed role right for you, or just a hot title?

Weigh the trade. You get customer impact and fast learning, but the work is high touch, may mean on site pressure, and does not scale like a product. Companies use it when each customer is different and the stakes are high.
The growth is real but from a small base, so treat 5,330 postings as a signal, not a guarantee. If you prefer deep platform work, a core data engineering role fits better.

show.title: Read the signal
items: Fast growth from a small base
Deep platform fans: stay core data engineering

beats.say: Either way, split your preparation. Half the loop is people and product, so give it half your time. Build a story linking business analytics, data engineering and agentic automation for a go to market team.

check.q: Which is the strongest reason to hesitate about a forward deployed role?
opts: It requires no coding
Work is high touch and customer specific, which suits some people less than deep platform work
Postings are falling quickly
check.why: The role trades scale and depth for customer proximity. If you prefer building shared platforms, core data engineering may suit you better.

work: List what you enjoy more: customer problems or platform internals, then pick targets.
Draft a two minute story that ties your analytics, data and automation work together.
Put equal time on behavioral and case practice in your weekly plan.

title: Ask before you build

beats.say: Your friend says, my car is slow, fix it. Do you start buying parts?
No. A good mechanic asks questions first. Slow when? Slow compared to what? Is it the engine, the tires, or the brakes?
Then the mechanic splits the trip into parts, guesses the likeliest culprit, and checks the cheapest thing first.
Interviewers hand you a vague problem the same way. If you draw a big system in two minutes, you have bought parts before listening. Ask, split, guess, then check.

check.q: An interviewer gives you a vague problem. What is the best first move?
opts: Draw the full architecture to show confidence
Ask who wants the answer and what they will do with it
Pick the tools you know best
Ask for the data and start querying
check.why: Knowing the goal and the user shapes everything after it. Drawing a system first is the classic way to fail this round.

work: Next time someone asks for a dashboard, ask what decision it will change before you open any tool.
Write the goal in one sentence and read it back to the requester.

title: Break down late deliveries

beats.say: A company says deliveries are late. Where do you start? Not with a diagram.

First, pin down late. Say it means more than fifteen minutes after the time promised at checkout, measured per delivery and reported as a rate. Write it down, because half the later arguments are about that sentence.
Next, split the journey: order placed, assigned to a driver, picked up, in transit, delivered. Lateness piles up in these stages, so you can ask what share of the delay happened in each.
Now guess, and rank. Too few drivers at peak, slow warehouses, bad promises, hard addresses. Rank by likely impact and how cheap each is to check.
Then ship the smallest useful thing: one table with time per stage for every delivery, and one chart by stage, site and hour. A few days of work.

check.q: What is the smallest valuable first deliverable for the late deliveries prompt?
opts: A real-time streaming platform
A table of time spent in each stage per delivery plus one chart of late rate by stage, site and hour
A machine learning model that predicts lateness
A list of all possible causes
check.why: It is quick, it attributes delay to stages, and it shows which hypothesis deserves deeper work.

work: Take a vague request this week and write the measure as one precise sentence before touching data.
Draw the process as stages and list where time can accumulate in each.

title: Where decomposition breaks

beats.say: Your analysis says drivers are the problem. Then the director says the data is wrong. What happened?
Often the measure was vague. Late against the promised time, or the time the customer expected? If you never agreed, two people can look at the same chart and disagree.

Next, timestamps. Stage times come from systems that nobody built for analysis. Drivers tap pickup late, or clocks differ between sites. Check which fields exist, which you trust, and which are missing, before you promise any chart.
Also watch averages. A stage with a small average delay can hide a few awful sites or hours. Split by site and hour, and compare rates, not raw counts.

check.q: Two people read the same late rate chart and disagree about its meaning. What is the most likely root cause?
opts: The chart type was wrong
The database was too slow
Late was never defined precisely and agreed
There was not enough data
check.why: Without an agreed definition such as more than 15 minutes after the checkout promise, the same numbers support different stories.

work: Before sharing an analysis, list each timestamp you used and note how it is captured and how far you trust it.
Always break headline rates down by site, hour and segment to catch hidden outliers.

title: Small first, big only when earned

beats.say: The interviewer pushes back: just build a real-time delivery platform. Do you say yes?
Probably not yet. A platform costs months and locks in guesses about what matters. A table and a chart cost days, and they tell you which guess is right.
Build bigger only when the small version proves the need, for example when the stage delays must be watched hourly to reassign drivers.

And define success up front: the late rate next month, compared with the same period before, for the changes made because of the analysis. Seasonality and promotions can fake an improvement, so compare like for like.

show.title: How you will know it worked
items: Only for changes the analysis drove

beats.say: When challenged, adjust openly. They score your thinking, and how you take pushback, not one answer.

show.sub: Scored on thinking and how you take a challenge

check.q: When is it right to move from the small table and chart to a larger platform?
opts: Immediately, to look ambitious
When the small analysis shows a recurring need, such as hourly monitoring to act on delays
Never, analysis should always stay manual
When the interviewer asks for it, without discussion
check.why: Investment should follow evidence of value. Earn the platform with a cheap result, and still adjust openly if the interviewer offers new constraints.

work: For any proposed platform, ask what a few-days version would teach you first.
Write the success measure with a before-and-after comparison on the same period before you start work.

title: Discovery is a doctor's visit

beats.say: A customer says, our report is too slow. Is slow really the problem?
Think of a doctor. A patient says, my stomach hurts. A good doctor does not hand over pills. She asks where, since when, and what have you tried already.
Discovery is the same. The customer gives you a symptom. You ask who will use this, what decision it changes, and what they do today. Then you write the answers down.
Last, say it back in two sentences. If they reply, not quite, celebrate. You just caught a wrong guess before building anything.

check.q: A customer says the report is too slow. What should you do first?
opts: Start tuning queries to speed it up
Ask who uses it and what decision it supports
Build a brand new dashboard tool
check.why: Slow is only a symptom. Asking who uses it and what decision it changes finds the real problem before you spend effort fixing the wrong thing.

work: Before your next customer call, write down the symptom they gave and three questions about it.
After the call, restate the problem in two sentences and send it to them.

title: The seven discovery questions

beats.say: You have one hour with a customer. What seven questions get you the real problem?
First, who will use it, and how often? Ten analysts daily is a different build from one executive monthly. Second, what decision will it change? If nobody can name one, stop and ask again.
Third, ask them to describe the screen or number they want. Fourth, what do they do today? A spreadsheet someone rebuilds every Monday shows what matters and where the data lives.

Fifth, what data exists, who owns it, how good is it? Sixth, constraints: security, deadlines, budget. Seventh, agree the success measure, like cutting prep from four hours to ten minutes, before you build.
Finish by restating in two sentences.

check.q: Why ask the customer to describe the screen or number they want to see?
opts: It lets you pick the chart colours
It turns a vague wish into a concrete definition of done
It proves the data is high quality
check.why: A described screen or number makes done concrete, so both sides can agree on what you are building before work starts.

work: Turn the seven questions into a one page template and fill it in during every first call.
For each project, write the success measure with a number, such as hours saved per week.

title: Why discovery goes wrong

beats.say: Why do customers ask for a dashboard, then reject it on delivery?
Because the symptom was never the problem. The ask for a faster report may hide a disagreement over what revenue means. Asking what decision it changes exposes that early.
Watch for three traps. The person in the room is not always the user. Their current workaround may use data nobody has checked. And the data owner may say yes, but the table is half empty.

show.title: Three traps
items: The person in the room is not the user
Owner says yes, table is half empty

beats.say: Verbal answers fade, so write them down and send them back the same day. Vague success, like better insight, cannot be tested. Push for a number and a date.

check.q: The data owner says yes, the data exists. What is the safest next step?
opts: Trust it and start building
Look at the actual table for gaps and quality
Ask the customer to sign off the design
check.why: Yes from an owner does not mean the data is complete or correct. Checking real data early stops surprises like half empty tables after you have built.

work: Ask to see a sample of the real data before you agree a deadline.
Confirm the person in the meeting is the actual user, or ask to meet one.
Replace vague goals like better insight with a measurable target in writing.

title: How much discovery is enough

beats.say: How much discovery is enough before you commit months of budget?
A day of questions is cheap beside a quarter of building the wrong thing. Spend the time where the risk is: unclear decision, unknown data quality, or locked systems.
Constraints shape the design. If you may not touch the source system, you copy data out instead of querying it live. A tight deadline may favour one thin report over a platform.
If the decision stays vague, do not build. Offer a one week prototype, or a data quality check, to buy clarity cheaply. Walking away from an unclear project is also a valid outcome.

show.title: When the decision is vague
items: Or run a data quality check

check.q: The customer cannot name a decision the work will change. What is the best move?
opts: Build a full platform to cover every case
Offer a small prototype or data check to find the need
Skip discovery and start from the data
check.why: Without a named decision the value is unproven. A small, cheap probe buys clarity without risking months of work.

work: Set a rule that no build starts until a decision and a measure are written down.
Price a short prototype or data check as a standard way to resolve unclear asks.

title: Cook one bowl first

beats.say: Would you build a whole restaurant before finding out if anyone likes your soup?
Engineers often do. They build the big general kitchen, with every dish, for every guest. Months later, the first real customer says, this is not what I needed.
The smarter move is small. One person, one decision, and their real ingredients. Cook one bowl of soup for one regular, and do it this week.
Then watch them taste it. Their reaction teaches you more than any menu you could plan. Everything else on the menu can wait until that person says, yes, this helps.

chip.text: Their feedback sets the next step

check.q: Why cook one bowl for one regular before building the full menu?
opts: It is cheaper to buy ingredients in small amounts
Their real reaction tells you what to build next
Big kitchens are always a bad idea
check.why: The point is fast learning from a real user. Early feedback stops you spending months on the wrong thing.

work: Name the one person and the one decision your next project serves.
Book a time this week to show them something rough.
Hold back features until that person has used the first version.

title: Five days to a first build

beats.say: What can you ship in five days that a customer will actually use?

show.sub: one user, one decision, real data

beats.say: Pick one user, such as a finance manager. Pick one decision, such as which of forty stores to restock on Monday. Pull a real extract, even just last ninety days, from the actual source.

Build the thinnest path. Load the file, clean it, draw one chart. No scheduler, no general framework. On day one, you find timestamps in three time zones. Fixing that now costs an hour. Finding it at launch costs weeks.

show.title: Thinnest path
show.note: Time zones found on day one: 1 hour to fix

beats.say: On day three, show the rough chart and ask what is wrong. Then write down what you did not build, and why.

show.title: Day three
items: List what you did not build

check.q: Why pull a real data extract on day one instead of using a clean sample?
opts: Real data loads faster
It exposes problems like mixed time zones while they are cheap to fix
The customer insists on it
check.why: Real data shows the customer's mess early. Fixing a time zone problem on day one costs an hour, but at launch it can cost weeks.

work: Pull a real extract before you design anything.
Set a rule: a rough chart on their data within three days.
Keep a not-built list next to the code.

title: Why the great demo broke

beats.say: Why does a demo that wowed everyone fall apart in week two?
Usually the demo ran on synthetic data. Real data has nulls, duplicates, late rows, and times in mixed zones. A clean fake file hides all of it, so the first real run breaks the story.

Another trap is the throwaway that becomes production. Someone relies on your hard coded script, and now it needs an owner. Say out loud that it is a prototype, and name what it lacks: no tests, no alerts, no retries.

show.title: Prototype, said out loud
items: Needs an owner if relied on

beats.say: The third trap is silent scope creep. Without a written not-built list, every request sounds small. Ten small yeses become the general system you meant to avoid.

check.q: A prototype built on real data is now used daily by the team. What is the best next step?
opts: Leave it, since it works
Name an owner and decide what to harden, such as tests and alerts
Rewrite it as a general platform
check.why: Once people depend on it, a prototype needs an owner and targeted hardening. A full rewrite into a platform is the over-building you set out to avoid.

work: Test every prototype against a real extract, not a hand-made file.
Label prototypes clearly and list what they lack.
Keep a written not-built list and review it with the customer.

title: When small is the wrong call

beats.say: When is building the smallest thing the wrong call?
It is right when the decision is uncertain and the user is reachable. The cost is low: one engineer, one week, and you learn what to build before spending a quarter.
It is wrong when the need is already proven, like regulatory reporting with fixed rules, or when a shortcut is unsafe, such as skipping access controls on personal data.
Choose your shortcuts carefully. Keep metric definitions and the data contract clean, because changing them later hurts everyone. Let the pipeline stay hacky because it is cheap to rebuild.

chip.text: Expensive to change vs cheap to rebuild

beats.say: After one user relies on it, generalise for the next two users, never for twenty imagined ones.

check.q: Which part of a first build should you keep clean even when everything else is rough?
opts: The scheduler
Metric definitions and the data contract
The chart colours
check.why: Definitions and contracts are what others build on, so changing them later is costly. A rough pipeline is cheap to rebuild.

work: Write down which parts of your next build are expensive to change, and protect them.
Skip the smallest-build approach where rules are fixed or security is at stake.
Plan generalising only when a second real user appears.

title: Telling a story so it lands

beats.say: How do you tell a friend about a disastrous trip so they truly understand it?

show.text: Tell it so they get it

beats.say: You say where you were, what you had to sort out, what you did, and how it ended. That is a STAR answer: situation, task, action, result.

chip.text: Same shape as a good trip story

beats.say: An interviewer is like that friend. They cannot see inside your head. They only believe what you describe, so describe what you personally did.

show.title: What the listener needs
items: They trust what you say you did

beats.say: Spend most of your time on the doing part. Keep the backstory to two sentences. Then finish with a number, like a nightly job cut from six hours to two, and one thing you learned.

check.q: In a STAR answer, which part should take the most time?
opts: The situation, so the listener has full context
The actions you personally took
The lessons learned
check.why: Actions are the evidence of what you can do. The situation should be about two sentences, and the result should be short and numeric.

work: Pick one project you are proud of and say it aloud in four sentences, one per STAR part.
Ask a colleague to listen and tell you what they think you personally did.

title: Spending your two minutes

beats.say: You get about two minutes for a behavioral answer. How do you spend them?
Situation: two sentences, about fifteen seconds. Task: the one thing you owned, about ten seconds. Say what was yours, not the team's.
Actions: about seventy seconds, the bulk. Walk through three or four decisions and why you made each. For example, you chose to backfill in batches because one big run would have starved the cluster.

show.title: Actions: decisions plus reasons
items: Why: one big run starves the cluster

beats.say: Result: one number, such as latency down from forty minutes to four, or two hundred thousand dollars saved a year. Close with what you learned, in one sentence.

show.sub: then one sentence on what you learned

check.q: Your answer is running long. What do you cut first?
opts: The decisions and reasons in the actions
Background detail in the situation
The number in the result
check.why: Context is the cheapest part to trim. Decisions and the measured result are the evidence being scored.

work: Time your best story with a clock and move the seconds toward the actions.
Write the one number for each story and how it was measured.

title: A story bank that covers everything

beats.say: Why can eight stories answer almost any behavioral question?

Because questions repeat in disguise. Ownership, conflict, failure, ambiguity, a tight deadline, mentoring, influencing without authority. Build a bank of eight to ten stories and tag each with every theme it can answer.
One outage story might fit failure, ownership, and a tight deadline. You only change which part you stress. Tell the same facts, lead with a different angle.

chip.text: Change the angle, not the facts

beats.say: Before each loop, map stories to the company's values. Amazon has leadership principles. Google prizes collaboration and humility. Atlassian prizes openness. Pick the story that proves the value.

check.q: Why tag each story with several themes?
opts: So you can reuse one story for different questions
So you can tell the story in less time
So you never need to rehearse
check.why: A question can show up in many forms. One well-known story, angled differently, covers several of them.

work: List eight to ten stories and tag each with at least three themes.
Before an interview, pick the top three stories for that company's stated values.

title: Why a polished story falls apart

beats.say: What makes a polished story fall apart in the first follow-up?
Saying we all the way through. If the interviewer cannot tell what you did, they score you on nothing. Say I for your decisions, and we for the team's results.

show.title: Ownership in your wording
items: I decided, I built, I argued

beats.say: Also a result with no number. Or a number you cannot defend. Every figure on your resume or in a story invites why, how measured, and compared to what. If you cannot answer, cut it.
A failure story needs a real failure, your part in it, and a changed habit. A fake weakness sounds rehearsed, and the interviewer will dig until it cracks.

check.q: An interviewer asks how you measured the 30 percent saving on your resume and you are unsure. Best move beforehand?
opts: Keep it, because numbers impress
Rework it to a figure you can explain, or cut it
Say it was approximate and move on
check.why: Each figure becomes a probing question. An undefended number damages trust in the rest of your claims.

work: For each resume number, write how it was measured and the baseline.
Rewrite one story replacing we with I where you made the decision.

title: Your career story, as a choice

beats.say: Twelve years of experience, but only four and a half as a data engineer. How do you answer that?
Say it first, briefly, as a choice. Never as an apology. An apology invites doubt, and a choice shows direction.

Use three parts. Where you started, such as the analytical side at Google, close to the people who used the data. Why you moved: you saw that pipelines decided what was possible. And what it gives you now.
The payoff is a design habit: you build pipelines around how the data will be used. Then stop talking and move to your strongest pipeline, with numbers.

check.q: What is the best way to handle the gap between total experience and data engineering title time?
opts: Hope nobody notices
Explain it briefly as a deliberate choice, then show strong pipeline work
Spend several minutes justifying each earlier role
check.why: A short, confident explanation removes doubt. Strong pipeline evidence then answers the real concern, which is capability.

work: Write your three-part career answer in under thirty seconds.
Prepare the handoff sentence that leads into your strongest pipeline.

title: Resume as an index to your stories

beats.say: Your resume is an index into your stories. So what goes first?
Lead each role with the biggest pipeline and its scale: rows a day, users served, dollars. Put a number in every bullet, but only ones you can defend in detail, because each one becomes a question.
Keep AI as a differentiator, but place it after the pipelines. Reliable data is the foundation, and leading with AI can sound like hype sitting on nothing.
Add your platform repository and the on-call agent as a project, with a link. A link lets the reader check the work, which beats any adjective.

check.q: Where should AI work sit on a data engineering resume?
opts: First, to stand out
After the strongest pipeline work, as a differentiator
Omitted, to avoid hype
check.why: Pipelines prove the foundation. AI after them reads as an extension of solid engineering, not a replacement for it.

work: Reorder each role so the largest pipeline and its scale come first.
Add the project link and confirm the repository reads clearly to a stranger.

title: Choosing and tailoring stories

beats.say: Is a bigger story bank always better?
No. Past ten, you cannot recall details under pressure, and a thin story collapses on the third follow-up. Eight deep stories beat twenty shallow ones.

At staff and architect level, choose stories by scope. Show decisions that crossed teams, trade-offs you weighed, and what you chose not to build. Influencing without authority matters more than heroics.

show.title: Staff-level evidence
items: What you chose not to build

beats.say: Tailor, but do not bend facts. Reorder which story leads for each company's values, and rehearse out loud until it takes two minutes, not five. Rambling costs more than a missing detail.

check.q: You are interviewing for a staff role. Which story is strongest?
opts: Working a weekend alone to fix an outage
Aligning three teams on a data contract and explaining the trade-offs
Finishing a ticket early
check.why: Staff roles are judged on scope and influence. Cross-team decisions with trade-offs show that, while solo heroics show individual effort.

work: Rank your stories by scope and keep the ones that crossed teams.
Rehearse the top three aloud and cut each to two minutes.

title: The inspector's tour

beats.say: How do you show you understand a pipeline you did not build, without writing any code?
Think of a house inspector. She does not start at the kitchen tap. She walks in the front door, then checks what comes in, what goes out, and each room in order.
She also says it aloud. This room is the laundry. Only then does she judge it. In an interview, that spoken tour proves you understand before you criticise.

show.title: Say it, then judge it
items: Only then say what is wrong

beats.say: Last, she asks what happens if something goes wrong. What if this runs twice? What if data arrives late?

check.q: In a code-reading round, what should you do first with each block of the pipeline?
opts: Point out what is wrong with it
Say aloud what it does, then judge it
Rewrite it in a cleaner style
check.why: Narrating purpose first shows you understand the code. Judging before understanding leads to wrong or shallow criticism.

work: Pick a pipeline you did not write and explain it aloud, top down, to a colleague.
Write one sentence of purpose for each block before reviewing it.

title: The satnav test

beats.say: Would you pass a driving test by blindly following the satnav?

show.text: Would you just follow the satnav?

beats.say: In some interviews, an AI assistant sits beside your code. It can only advise. You still hold the wheel, and you type every line.
The examiner is watching for one thing. Do you notice when the satnav says turn into a lake? Reading its answer, questioning it, and saying why you accept it is the skill being graded.
So read the map first, check each instruction before you turn, and talk through your choices. And some companies ban the satnav entirely, so ask beforehand.

show.sub: And ask if AI is allowed

check.q: Why would an interviewer mark you down for pasting in an assistant's answer?
opts: The answer was too long
They cannot see that you understood or verified it
Assistants are always wrong
check.why: The interviewer grades your judgment, and they can only judge what they hear and see you do. Unexplained pasting shows none of it.

work: Practise saying aloud why you accept or change each suggestion from an AI tool.
Before any interview, ask the recruiter whether AI is allowed in that round.

title: Reading a pipeline top down

beats.say: You are handed two hundred lines of someone else's pipeline. Where do you even start?

Top down. First the entry point, the job that kicks everything off. Then inputs: which tables or files it reads. Then outputs: what it writes and where. Only then walk each transformation, one block at a time.
Say each block's purpose aloud before judging it. For example: this joins fifty million orders to customers, then sums revenue by day.

show.title: Narrate a block
show.text:
join orders to customers
group by order_date
sum revenue
show.note: 50 million orders in, one row per day out

beats.say: Now review. Run it twice: does the output double? Is it incremental, or does it reread everything? Does it do what the business wants? What does it cost? What about nulls and late rows?

check.q: A job appends yesterday's rows to a table every run. What does the rerun question expose?
opts: Running it twice duplicates the rows
It will be too slow
It reads the wrong tables
check.why: Appending without a key or partition overwrite means a retry or rerun inserts the same rows again, so totals double.

work: Use the five review questions on a pipeline at work and write down the answers.
Practise reading code in the order: entry, inputs, outputs, transforms.

title: Inside the one-hour AI round

beats.say: What actually happens in a one-hour round with an AI assistant?
There are three phases. First, fix a bug. Second, implement a feature. Third, optimise against harder tests. The assistant sits in a chat panel next to a multi-file codebase.
It cannot edit your files. You write the code. Graders score problem solving, code quality, how well you verify the assistant's suggestions, and communication.
Your loop: read the code first, ask for explanations, write specific prompts naming the function, constraint and input shape, read every suggested line, then run tests.
Add one edge-case test of your own. It proves you checked.

check.q: Which prompt is best to give the assistant?
opts: Fix this bug
In parse_orders, handle rows with a null customer_id, input is a list of dicts
Write the whole feature for me
check.why: A good prompt names the function, the constraint and the input shape, so the answer is targeted and easy to check.

work: Practise a timed hour with three phases using any coding assistant, typing all code yourself.
Write a prompt template: function, constraint, input shape.

title: When the assistant is confidently wrong

beats.say: The assistant gives you code that looks perfect and passes your test. Why can that still sink you?
Because candidates who leaned on it without showing understanding were marked down. The grader cannot see your thoughts. Silence looks like copying.
Plausible code hides bugs. Say it suggests an inner join. Customers with no orders vanish from the report, and nobody notices unless you checked.

show.title: A quiet bug
show.text:
customers inner join orders
-- customers with zero orders disappear

beats.say: Defence: read every line before typing, say why you accept or change it, and run tests often. A suggestion you cannot explain is a suggestion you should not type.

show.title: Defences
items: Say why you accept or change it
Never type what you cannot explain

check.q: The assistant's code passes all current tests. What is the best next move?
opts: Move on to save time
Explain why it works and add an edge-case test of your own
Ask the assistant if it is correct
check.why: Passing tests only proves the cases already covered. Explaining it and adding your own edge case shows real verification.

work: After any AI-written code, add one test for an input the existing tests miss.
Practise narrating accept or change decisions out loud while coding.

title: Why strong engineers miss the break

beats.say: In a code-reading round, why do strong engineers still miss the bug?
They judge too early. They spot something odd in block two and start fixing before they know what the pipeline is for.
Typical hidden faults: an append that duplicates rows on rerun, a date filter using local time while data is in UTC, a join that silently drops null keys.
Also remember: you are not writing new code. The task is explain, find the break, propose a refactor. Name the failure, say when it triggers, then give the smallest fix.

check.q: Which finding is best phrased for a code-reading round?
opts: This code is messy
On a retry the load appends again, so day totals double. Overwrite that day's partition instead
I would rewrite everything in another language
check.why: It names the failure, the trigger and a small fix, which is what the round asks for.

work: Read a teammate's job and list each hidden-fault type above that could apply.
Practise stating every finding as failure, trigger, smallest fix.

title: Refactor, don't rewrite

beats.say: You found five problems in the pipeline. Do you rewrite it?
Usually no. A rewrite costs weeks, risks new bugs and delays everything else. Rank fixes by risk removed per effort.

show.title: Rank by risk removed per effort

beats.say: Make reruns safe first, for example overwrite one day's partition instead of appending. That stops duplicate data. Then incremental loads, which cut a full reread of, say, two terabytes to one day's slice.
Rewrite only when the design itself is wrong, like batch logic for a need that is truly real time. Always state what you would measure to prove the fix worked.

show.title: Rewrite only if
items: The design fits the need badly
Patches cost more than the rebuild

check.q: A pipeline duplicates rows on rerun and also rereads 2 TB daily. What do you propose first?
opts: Rewrite in a new framework
Make the load idempotent, then make it incremental
Add more compute
check.why: Correctness comes first and is a small change. Incremental loading then cuts cost. A rewrite is slower and riskier.

work: For your own pipelines, rank known problems by risk removed per effort.
Prepare a one-sentence success metric for each proposed fix.

title: AI policy and how to prepare

beats.say: Is using AI in an interview smart or cheating? It depends on the company.
Prep sites report Amazon treats undisclosed AI use as cheating. Meta, Google and Canva run rounds where it is expected.
So the safe move is to ask each recruiter, for each round. Never assume. A wrong guess can end your process.

Then practise both ways. Without help, to prove your fundamentals. With help, to show judgment: explain first, prompt narrowly, verify everything. Both skills are tested; which one depends on the room.

show.title: Practise both
items: With AI: explain, prompt narrowly, verify
Know which room you are in

check.q: You are unsure whether AI is allowed in a round. What should you do?
opts: Use it quietly, since others do
Avoid it and hope
Ask the recruiter before the round
check.why: Policies differ widely, and undisclosed use can be treated as cheating. Asking removes the risk.

work: Email each recruiter to ask what AI policy applies to every round.
Schedule practice sessions with AI and without it each week.

title: One goal number, and what must not break

beats.say: Your lemonade stand sold more cups today. Is that good news? Not if you gave every cup away free.
A north star metric is the one number that shows real value to customers. For a ride app, that is completed trips per week. The whole team tries to push it up.

But pushing one number can break something else. So you add guardrails. These are numbers that must not get worse, like cancellations and support tickets. Optimise clicks with no guardrail on purchases, and you get more clicks and less money.

check.q: A team pushes click-through up 20 percent. Which extra number best protects against a hollow win?
opts: Page load time only
A guardrail such as purchases or revenue
Number of team members
Total page views
check.why: A guardrail on a value outcome like purchases shows whether the extra clicks produced real value or just noise.

work: Write down the north star for your product in one sentence and name who owns it.
List two or three guardrails next to every goal metric on your team dashboard.

title: Stickiness and funnels with real numbers

beats.say: Ten thousand people use your app this month, but only two thousand show up on a given day. Is that healthy?
Daily active users divided by monthly active users is stickiness. Two thousand over ten thousand is twenty percent. It means the average monthly user comes back about six days in thirty.

A funnel shows where people drop out. A thousand impressions, fifty clicks, ten add to cart, four purchases. Each step has a pass rate, five percent, twenty percent, forty percent. Compare them to see where to dig.

check.q: DAU is 3,000 and MAU is 12,000. What is stickiness and what does it mean?
opts: 25 percent, a monthly user is active about 7 or 8 days a month
4 percent, users rarely return
25 percent, 25 percent of users churn
300 percent, very high growth
check.why: 3,000 divided by 12,000 is 25 percent, so the average monthly user appears on roughly a quarter of the days.

work: Compute stickiness for your main product and track it weekly next to MAU.
Build a funnel table with count and step pass rate, not just the overall end-to-end rate.

title: Clicks up, conversion down: what happened?

beats.say: Click-through rose ten percent, but conversion fell five percent. Did the new recommender help or hurt?

First, check the definition. If conversion means purchases per click, extra low-intent clicks drag it down, even while total purchases rise. So compute purchases per impression. That is the number the business actually cares about.

chip.text: Per click fell, per impression rose

beats.say: Then segment by user type, product, device and position. A win for one group can hide a loss in another. Look at what happens after the click: bounce rate, time on page, relevance.

show.title: Dig into the change
items: Segment: user type, product, device, position
After the click: bounce rate, time on page

beats.say: Last, check the experiment itself. Was the split clean?

show.sub: Check assignment before trusting any lift

check.q: Click-through rises and conversion per click falls. What should you compute first?
opts: Average session length
Purchases per impression
Number of new accounts
Total clicks only
check.why: Purchases per impression does not shift when click volume changes, so it shows whether the algorithm made more sales from the same traffic.

work: Write the exact denominator next to every rate metric in your dashboard.
When a metric moves, run a segment breakdown by device, user type and position before explaining it.

title: Why peeking at an A/B test fools you

beats.say: You run an A B test, check it daily, and stop the moment it looks significant. Why is that a trap?

A five percent significance threshold accepts a one in twenty fluke for a single look. Every extra look is another chance for noise to cross the line. Check often and the real false positive rate climbs well above five percent.

show.title: False positive rate by number of looks

beats.say: So fix the primary metric, guardrails and sample size before you start, based on the smallest effect worth detecting. Then run at least one full week, because weekday and weekend users behave differently.

show.title: Plan before you run
items: Fix primary metric and guardrails up front
Size the sample from the smallest effect worth detecting
Run at least one full weekly cycle
Do not stop early on a good-looking result

check.q: Why does checking significance daily and stopping at the first good result cause problems?
opts: It makes the sample too large
Each look adds a chance of a false positive, so the error rate inflates
It biases the random assignment
Daily checks slow the experiment
check.why: Every peek is another draw of random noise, so the chance that at least one looks significant by luck grows well beyond five percent.

work: Write the sample size and end date into the experiment doc before launch.
If you must monitor early, use a sequential testing method built for repeated looks.

title: Sample ratio mismatch: the split that lies

beats.say: You planned a fifty fifty split. The dashboard says fifty-three, forty-seven. Close enough?
On a small sample, yes, chance explains it. On millions of users, no. That gap is a sample ratio mismatch, and it means assignment or logging is broken.
Maybe a bug crashes the new version before it logs events, so unhappy users vanish from one arm. Then the groups are no longer comparable, and any lift you see is biased.
So test the ratio first, with a chi-squared test. If it fails, fix the pipeline and rerun. Do not read the result.

show.sub: If it fails, fix and rerun

check.q: A 50/50 test on 2 million users shows 51.5/48.5 and the check fails. What is the right action?
opts: Ship the winner anyway
Drop the smaller arm
Investigate assignment and logging, fix, and rerun
Wait a week and recheck
check.why: A significant ratio mismatch means the arms are not comparable, so results cannot be trusted until the cause is fixed.

work: Add an automatic sample ratio check to every experiment report.
When it fails, compare drop-off by browser, device and app version to find the cause.

title: Randomise where users affect each other

beats.say: You test a new driver matching algorithm. Randomise by user, and you may learn nothing. Why?
Because drivers are shared. If treated riders grab the nearby drivers, control riders wait longer. The control group is hurt by the treatment, so the measured gap is wrong.

Instead, randomise by city, or by time window, so each arm has its own pool of drivers. The cost is fewer units. With twenty cities you have twenty data points, not millions, so you need larger effects or longer runs.
Rule of thumb: randomise at the level where users affect each other, and pay for it in power.

show.sub: Pay for it in statistical power

check.q: Which design best fits a test of a ride-matching change where riders compete for the same drivers?
opts: Randomise by individual rider
Randomise by city or time window
Randomise by phone model
Skip testing and compare before and after
check.why: Randomising by city or time window keeps each arm's driver pool separate, so one arm cannot change the other's outcome.

work: List which of your features create interference between users, such as shared inventory, pricing or supply.
For those, plan geo or time-based tests and budget for longer runs because there are fewer units.
